Now, Mr. Speaker, closely associated with the woollen industry of Canada is the sheepraising business. We have a lot of fine sheep in my riding, and many of the farmers are very proud of what they have accomplished in this regard. If the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) would pay less attention to wiping out the tariff and more attention to the development of the sheep industry as well as some of the other branches of industry that come under his jurisdiction, it might be better for his department and, incidentally, for the agricultural development of Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What would my
hon. friend suggest should be done?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will
make the suggestion before I close my remarks in regard to this item. That we can raise good sheep in Canada is shown by the fact that at the greatest show of live stock in the world, the Chicago International Stock Show, sheep bred in Canada swept the board of prizes last year, and every year they meet with similar success. This proves that Canadian sheep are right and that the wool is right. And yet we have only 2,600,000 sheep as compared with Great Britain with its small area, where there are 25,000,000 sheep. I wish the Minister of Agriculture to listen to this, for I am sure it will interest him. In the

3206	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Armstrong (Lambton)
United States there are over 40,000,000 sheep, an increase in one year of 1,358,000, while in Canada the number of our sheep decreased by
400,000	since this government took office.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What was the reason?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is up
to the Minister of Agriculture to say. In Australia there are 80,000,000 sheep while in Canada we have only 2,600,000.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mostly in
western Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I wish to call another matter to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture. In Canada we raise only 15 per cent of the 70,000,000 pounds of wool that we use every year. Surely we can find some way whereby to increase our flocks and help fill that order for 70,000,000 pounds of wool per year.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend
surely knows that the wool we import is not of the same quality as that which we grow.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister knows very well that 15 per cent of the 70,000,000 pounds of wool is an amount so small that it is hardly worth considering. Three quarters of that total amount of wool could easily be produced in Canada. This government has reduced the duty on Australian mutton and lamb to one-half cent per pound, thus flooding our markets with these products. Canadian mutton and lamb are second to none in quality and flavour for table use, and there is no necessity to import them. Yet the Canadian duties were recently lowered from three cents to one-half cent per pound to encourage the sale in Canada of lamb and mutton grown by the farmers of Australia.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would the hon.
member tell the House how the importation of mutton last year compares with that of 1921 and 1922?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have
not those statistics at hand.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They were in
the same book referred to by my hon. friend for his other figures.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am
merely making statements which I am prepared to back up.
There is another industry in my riding in which the farmers are particularly interested, and that is the growing of sugar beets. I have already put on record my position in regard to this industry, which has received unfair treatment at the hands of this govern-lMx. J. E. Armstrong.]
ment, but I would like to add a few words to what I have already said. Without investigation or a word of warning this same Finance Minister reduced the duty on refined sugar one-half cent per pound. Owing to this reduction thousands of farmers whose livelihood depended on this industry were at once notified by the large sugar refineries of Wallaceburg and Chatham that the price they received would be reduced by 50 cents per ton. The hon. member for Kent, Ontario, (Mr. Chaplin) told the House only yesterday of the effect of this cut in his riding. He told how a few years ago, before this government tampered with the tariff, there were
40,000	acres of sugar beets under cultivation in his riding, from which the farmers received $4,000,000; $2,000,000 was paid for labour, making a total of $6,000,000 expended in his riding. Last year the acreage totalled 30,000, and he said this year it would probably amount to 20,000. My district is right alongside that of the hon. member for Kent. Ontario, and anything affecting his part of the western peninsula also affects my district. The loss to these farmers has been enormous, but on top of it all, as though the Finance Minister wanted to discourage further the Canadian beet producer and make it still more difficult for him to engage in the production of sugar beets at any profit, by the treaties with Australia and the West Indies he reduced the duty on raw sugar coming in from those countries one cent per pound. Australia sent in last year 26.000.000 pounds of raw sugar; the West Indies sent in last year 17,000,000 pounds of raw sugar, and they are now put in a position whereby they can pour in the raw sugar at an altogether lower cost, and undermine another great basic industry of our country.
Look for a moment at the position in which our sugar beet growers are placed and the competition they are up against. In the production of sugar beets practically the whole profit comes from the hard work of weeding, hoeing, planting and marketing the beets, which means months of work for everyone on the farm. If the sugar beet growers in Canada have to hire help, they are compelled to pay from $5 to $7 per da}' for men to do this kind of work. These men work with their backs bent close to the ground with a hoe, the handle of which is only a foot long; hour after, hour and day after day they work in that position. Compare their wages with the wages paid in the West Indies or Australia for similar labour. The help provided in the West Indies comes from the second lowest class of civilization in the world; the workers receive less than

The Budget-Mr. Armstrong (Lambton)
$1 per day and live on the cheapest possible food; a handful of rice is k good meal. Their clothing consists of a pair of overalls with a string for suspenders, and if sufficiently optimistic the string is not needed. By the action of the government in thus lowering the duty on raw sugar coming into Canada from these countries, Canadian raw sugar has had a proportionate drop in price, so the government has been wholly responsible for the reduced price paid to Canadian beet growers.
If farmers in the west can produce sugar beets successfully as the minister claims they can-and I am delighted to hear that statement-why not protect them and their market? There is no reason why we should not produce in Canada practically all the raw sugar we need, but to-day we only produce 10 per cent of our own requirements. Why not compel other countries to pay for access to our market? Why oblige Canadian growers to take less for their product and to compete with cheap labour in West Indies and Australia? -We protect the manufacturer against cheap labour; why not the beet grower?
Some weeks ago I asked for information in regard to the raw sugar coming from the West Indies, and the minister asked that it stand as an order for return. I sent away for the information and received a reply inside of three days, the accuracy of which I am prepared to vouch for. Field labourers in the West Indies are paid approximately $1 per day, which is probably the scale of wages paid in Australia as well. The freight rate on sugar from the British West Indies to St. John is 18 cents per hundred pounds net, and to Montreal 22 cents. The present c.i.f. price of British West Indies sugar is S3.25 to $3.30 at St. John, and 5 cents higher to Montreal; deduct 18 cents to 20 cents for the price at point of shipment. Under the present West Indies trade agreement now being discussed in this House the rate of duty on raw sugar from the British West Indies is to be 28.712 cents per hundred pounds, on a basis of 96 degrees polarization, as against a former rate of 45 cents. I would like hon. gentlemen to listen carefully to this next statement. This gives a preference in the duty on raw sugar produced in the British West Indies of 1 cent per pound. It is understood that the rate of duty on Australian raw sugar will be the same, although not specifically mentioned in the tariff. This will mean that the Canadian growers of sugar beets will receive $1 less per ton, and you can imagine how they will appreciate such a reduction.
Another very extensive industry in my riding is the dairy and cattle industry. The Finance minister, owing to the treaty arrangements entered into with Australia and New Zealand, has placed that industry in a most precarious position. Canada has imported over 5,000,000 pounds of butter this year from those countries, and the market of the Canadian farmer has been undermined. The Minister of Finance knows very well that if our farmers had been protected in this regard during the past few months hundreds of thousands of dollars which have gone to swell the profits of the cattle men and butter makers of Australia and New Zealand would have been in their pockets.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Where would the
butter have come from?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We can
produce plenty of butter in Canada to supply our home consumption.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not at a moment's notice.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Canada exported 25,000,000 pounds. Let me go a little further and I will show where this butter will come from. The minister knows full well that he has opened our doors to the products of these countries, and has thereby compelled our people to accept less for their products than they otherwise would have received had the home market been kept for them.
During my address on the Speech from the Throne the Minister of Agriculture said that the importation of butter this year would not exceed 1,000,000 pounds. We told him then that he was mistaken. What does he think now, when our imports have amounted to more than 5,000,000 pounds of butter in four months of this year? Has he any idea when these shipments will cease, or is he in the least concerned? No! Let me just call his attention to a statement made by one of the largest creameries in western Ontario dated April 12 of this year, which statement could no doubt be duplicated in almost any creamery in Canada:
With the huge shipments of Australian and New Zealand butter pouring in, and with the butter exports of our nortJh-west out off from the United States by the new United States duty of 12 cents per pound, our market has crashed, as we have been expecting it to crash for the past month.
As an example, we sold to one firm last week 100 boxes of prints at 451 cents f.o.b. They called us up this .morning and stated that they could only pay 421 cents, and this afternoon they called again and advised us that they had been offered butter, as they stated, from the largest creamery in Toronto, at 41 cents delivered. We finally were compelled to sell them 80 boxes at 401 cents.
3208	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Armstrong (Lambton)
I am enclosing you a couple of letters we received this morning that wall show you how the Montreal and Toronto markets are.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then they have not sold 100 boxes at all? The hon. member said they had sold them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How
could they sell them? The price was going down and down all the time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Prices went up all January.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How much higher would they have been if it had not been for the millions of pounds of Australian and New Zealand butter coming into this country?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the production of butter in Canada?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I placed those figures on Hansard in the statement I made in the debate on the Speech from the Throne. The amount is 280,000,000 pounds, if I remember correctly. It is an ample supply to furnish the whole Canadian market during the whole year.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the duty on butter coming in from Australia at present?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: One cent a pound. But if you were to send Canadian butter to Australia you would have to pay a duty of 8 cents per pound, and if it was going to the United States you would have to pay a duty of 12 cents a pound, for they have raised their duty within the last few months from 8 to 12 cents a pound? Why? To protect their farmers.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Was not the duty raised here also on butter coming in from Australia?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not at all. The hon. gentleman has in mind the dumping clause. It is true that when the government found these enormous supplies of Australian butter coming in, they thought they would put a stop to it by applying the dumping clause, but even the dumping clause did not keep it out, as the hon. gentleman knows. Does not the hon. gentleman believe that if the Canadian market had been protected at a reasonable rate, Australian and New Zealand butter would not have come into this country in such large quantities?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We were very glad to get their butter because we had only ten days' (supply on hand.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is the hon. gentleman's way of putting it. Similar statements are made about the food supplies in the Motherland, that they have only sufficient for eight days or so. But how can the hon. gentleman say that?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: England's supplies keep on coming in to that country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
So does the butter keep on coming in here. I have a letter here from Alex. D. McGillis and Company, produce brokers, Montreal, who says in regard to butter:
This has been a disastrous week, with the disastrous decline entailing heavy losses on account of recent arrivals of Australian butter.
J. M. Ham, commission broker, Toronto, says:
Due to heavy arrivals of foreign butter, and liberal shipments of fresh made from western Canada on consignment, butter prices on all markets have sdmply collapsed this week. The decline started in Montreal on Monday, and each day, in fact several times during a day, prices have gone lower.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does the hon.
member want to keep out the western Canada butter as well as the Australian butter?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not at all. I am as proud as the hon. member is that western Canada is producing butter in such large quantities. I am president of a creamery company that was in the habit of shipping to the northwest and to British Columbia car after car of butter, from our district in years gone by. I am glad to know that you are able to produce butter in the west to supply this market, but for the good of the farming community in old Ontario I ask you to help us protect our home market in order that we can carry on and give the farmers of this province a fair return.
While the Australian and New Zealand butter was pouring into this country by millions of pounds Arnold's of Toronto, the large distributors of groceries in that city, carried this half-page advertisement in a Toronto newspaper dated April 8, 1926:
Butter six cents a pound lower than last week.
30,000 pounds Cottage Brand Creamery Butter.
That was a drop of six cents a pound in a few days. This butter had come in from Australia and New Zealand, where the farmers did not have to keep their cattle in the bam in winter and feed them hay and chop.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does not butter
always drop at that time of the year?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Why
should it drop in Canada? Our cows have to

be housed and fed and cared for, but in Australia and New Zealand they do not need to house their catttle and feed them as we have to do ours. That is one reason why out farmers should be protected.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What was the price of
butter last year?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have
answered a lot of questions, but I am not a walking encyclopaedia.
Now just a word on the automobile industry. This is another industry that has been vitally affected since the present Minister of Finance took office. Not only has the automobile industry suffered at his hands, but the Canadian Manufacturers' Association have stated that one thousand other industries that supply parts to the automobile factories have been vitally affected. Millions of dollars' worth of orders that have been placed in these factories have been cancelled. I know of one factory alone that has had over a million dollars' worth of orders cancelled since this budget came down. You must remember, too that some 3,600 agents and garage men have already made their purchase of new cars for the year 1926, and their stock of old cars is only just beginning to move. The estimate of loss to these men, from a reliable source, is over five million dollars. Sales of Canadian-made automobiles in 1925 amounted to $107,000,000; at least 25,000 employees were engaged in the business of manufacturing motors, and 100.000 people were dependent on the industry and its allied industries. The tariff was changed without any warning, without a public investigation as promised in the Speech from the Throne and on the public platform by many of the members on the opposite side of the House. I am not going to argue that the duty on automobiles and trucks was too high or too low, because speaking frankly, I do not know, and I have no means of knowing, nor have the members on the opposite side of the House who are making hearsay arguments in regard to this industry. I do, however, condemn the action of this government, which after having appointed a tariff board for the purpose of getting just such information regarding industries, should deliberately cut the tariff on these goods over 40 per cent without consulting the tariff board.
The motor manufacturers have presented a reasonable request to this government, that before any definite action be taken in connection with this budget their industry should be investigated by the tariff board now appointed. Surely this is a reasonable request and should not be ignored by the govern-

The Budget-Mr. Armstrong (Lambton)
ment. The statement I make in this regard is borne out by an u appeal " which is to be found in The Labor Leader, Toronto, dated April 23, 1926. The statement is surmounted by heavy headlines and is published in black type, indicating the importance with which it is regarded. Surely hon. gentlemen opposite do not think this paper is influenced by any, but the best of motives. The statement reads, as follows:
An appeal to the members of House of Commons of Canada.
Representing, as you jdo, the citizens of this great Dominion, "The Labour Leader" on behalf of the men who work in the Canadian automoobile factories and the various factories that make parts and accessories, numbering about twenty-five thousand, with: about one hundred thousand women and childrens dependent upon them, earnestly request you to refer-' the clause in the budget that deals with the tariff on motor cars to the new tariff commission, so that these workers may have an opportunity of placing their views before them. Gentlemen, forget your political parties, and lend a hand to these hardworking toilers.
In closing let me say that one of the worst features of the action of the King government in its tinkering with the tariff is the fact that the existence of every industry is threatened and all business is made uncertain. Few manufacturing plants or large industries will spend money or invest capital in improvements or branching out. There is no certainty as to the future for them. The fact that a tariff commission was appointed led people to suppose there might be tariff changes. The people were more or less prepared for that. Eight days after a tariff commission was appointed the government, apparently ignoring the commission and without any investigation, made radical changes in the tariff regarding certain industries.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Cut out the tariff.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
An hon.
gentleman from Saskatchewan says " cut out the tariff". That is the same old story. It means the adoption of a policy which will destroy our industries and drive our people from this country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Will the hon.
gentleman permit me a question? He has been very good-natured and very courteous and kind and I appreciate that very much. The question I desire to ask is this: How does he account for the enormous increase in production and in trade during the last four years if all the industries of the country have been ruined, as he and some of his friends have been arguing?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There has been no increase.
3210	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Armstrong (Lambton)

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, a tremendous increase.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman who has just asked the question realizes to the full that the Minister of Finance in his budget speech distinctly gave credit to Providence for the wonderful development in this country during the past year-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: All of it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-and if the hon. gentleman follows up the suggestion of the Finance minister he will know why it was that the farming industry in particular was able to accomplish what it did.
Now, to revert to what I was saying when I was interrupted, the fact that a tariff board was to exist gave some promise of business stability. But if that board is to be ignored in regard to certain industries, why ask its decision as to any industry at all? Why have a tariff board at all, with all the added expense it entails, if it is not to investigate and report on all industries?
The Minister of Finance, when addressing the automobile delegation at the Keith theatre recently, said he would " stick to his guns " before he even heard what the deputation had to say. Will he be equally as drastic with the tariff commission?
In conclusion may I say that there never was a time when there was greater need of tariff stability in this country? Canada requires capital to develop her mines and woodlands, her water powers and her industries, and to give employment to her people. But what incentive has foreign capital, or for that matter any capital, to invest in Canada while we have a government that will not give a reasonable stability to business and does not inspire confidence in business people? The King government, through the negotiation of foreign treaties and the tariffs, has struck a blow at the industries of Canada and at her basic industry, agriculture, at a most unfortunate time. As long as the present government is in office, our industries, if they live at all, will exist in a state of insecurity. The fate of the various industries which I have mentioned is likely to be the fate of other industries under the King government, and so long as this government holds sway we cannot hope for improved industrial conditions in Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the present debate, which has lasted now for about four weeks, we have been treated .to a discussion on almost every subject under the sun. The coal question has been debated, also matters pertaining to the

production of wheat, oil, motor cars, and sugar-beets, as well as that hardy annual the Australian treaty. In the few remarks which I propose to offer I desire to prescribe for the House a diet of fish. Fish, they say, i3 a brain food, and as the constituency which I represent is one of the great fish-producing areas of this Dominion I shall devote some little attention to that great basic industry.
At the outset I congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on the splendid budget which he has presented. It is a most excellent budget, and I have received many letters, and some telegrams, from the people of my constituency expressing their approval of it. One of the outstanding features of the budget is its strength; it is a strong budget. We have been told by members of the House who are in a position to know, that this is the best budget that has been submitted in the last twenty-five years. The amendment offered to it is a relatively weak amendment.
Since last October we have heard a great deal from the Conservative party, and we have read much in the Conservative press, as to the hopeless and weak position of the King government. In the same quarters the present budget is referred to as an election budget. I think that is responsible for the uneasiness of hon. gentlemen opposite. The budget is a good election budget, it is one upon which we can win an election at. any time we appeal to the country. We have been told in the Conservative press and by speakers on Conservative platforms that this government is a very weak one. I ask how it is possible for a weak government to win all its by-elections?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I ask how it is possible for it to strengthen its position in the House of Commons-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It has not done so yet.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-and also to strengthen itself very materially in the country at large. If this is the weak, vaccilating government which our Conservative friends would have the people believe it is, how did it ever muster up sufficient strength and courage to apply the closure in this House? If it is such a weak government, how did it manage to negotiate treaties the operation of which is increasing our favourable trade balance and our standing in the financial world? We found when this government came into office in 1921 that there had been an adverse trade balance of $29,000,000. In 1922 we had a favourable trade balance of $6,000,000. In

The Budget-Mr. Stork
1923, it rose to $142,000,000, in 1924 to $165,000,000, in 1925,	$284,000,000, and
as disclosed in the Robb budget the favourable trade balance amounts to $401,000,000. Now, Mr. Speaker, bow can a claim be made that this is a weak government and the country is going to the dogs under Liberal administration, and at the same time how can the Conservative party lay such great claims to the strength of their own party and their position, when the best they can do is to submit to this House the weakest amendment that has ever been submitted to the House in the last thirty-five years? The reduction in taxation, the reduction in the postage, the splendid Canadian National statement and the treatment of automobile duties have all been dealt with at considerable length. The duty on automobiles has caused a great deal of discussion in this House. The Conservative party has always stood for a high tariff, but I feel that they must regard themselves as being in a most unfortunate position at this particular time. They have been telling the people of Canada, that industry was going to rack and ruin, that if we tampered with the duty on automobiles that industry would close up. The hon. member who has just addressed the House (Mr. Armstrong, Lambton) has made the usual complaint about the effect of tariff reduction on the industries of this country. The party which insists on saving the country by keeping the tariff high and by jacking up the duties has told us that these automobile industries will be ruined. Having appointed themselves the guardians of the country, they must feel very badly let down when they find the man who makes more motor cars than all the rest of the automobile manufacturers together-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Where does he make
them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A lot of them in Windsor.
This gentleman tells us he does not require the assistance of any tariff for his business. He says the industry does not require a tariff and he himself is in favour of free trade. That is going even one better than any of us. I have before me an item printed in the Toronto Globe of April 21, dated at Windsor, which reads:
Henry Ford, Detroit automobile magnate, to-day dealt a hefty blow at high tariff to protect his Canadian industry, when he told The Globe during a brief interview at the Walkervnlle ferry dock that the plant in Ford City would run*better under free trade.
'T am a free trader," Mr. Ford said. "It was not necessary for you to ask me that," he continued. "Mr. Campbell said the Canadian factory would continue to operate, and it is my belief the factory would

speechtext:
One great benefit accruing
to the Dominion under the provisions of the present budget is the fact that, for all time to come it places in its grave the ghost of the whisper of death. A great deal of time has been spent ,and a great deal of newspaper ink has been used in trying to prove to the people of Canada that the whisper of death prevails in the whole of this great country. So far as the province of British Columbia is concerned there is no whisper of death west of the Rocky mountains. British Columbia does not swallow propaganda in regard to this country going to smash simply because the Tory party is not in power guiding the affairs of the great Dominion of Canada.
Even the hon. member for East Lambton, brought up again the claim of injury resulting from the Australian treaty. The Australian treaty has had a marvellous effect upon the prosperity of British Columbia. I wish to quote briefly from a newspaper which I think no one can accuse of being particularly favourable to the Liberal party in that province. I quote from the Vancouver Province of Tuesday, November 3, 1925, just a few days after the general election. I will not quote the whole extract. It goes on to outline what will happen in the way of development in British Columbia and it winds up with this statement:
The King government, during its four years in office, has not had many opportunities of serving the country in a Abroad and constructive way, but the negotiation of the treaty with Australia, is one good work which stands to its credit.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock I was proceeding to say that this government has been largely responsible for the prosperity which the province of British Columbia is now enjoying. I have in my hand a newspaper to which I am sure our friends opposite will take no exception; it is the Mail and Empire. It contains a half page advertisement headed "A young giant still expanding." Appearing in such a paper, I am sure the House will agree with me that it should have the effect of knocking off the funeral plumes from that defunct Canada which the Tory party has been so eager to convey to its political graveyard. After setting forth the prosperity in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, it has this to say of British Columbia :
British Columbia is in the throes of the greatest development in iher history. The visitor of any of her cities or towns feels this the 'moment he steps off the train or steamboat. This great pulsating throb of new life is reflected in heavy investments in buildings and commercial enterprises arising out of her basic wealth in mines, forests, fisheries and the fruits of the Bodl.
That, I believe, is a fair statement of fact. British Columbia is enjoying a wonderful period of prosperity. The Toronto Globe of yesterday contains a short editorial headed, "How it helps the west," and I have no doubt the House will be interested to hear it. It reads:
Additional vindication of the Canadian-Australian preferential treaty, if such were needed, is seen in the impetus which it is giving <to the paper and pulp industry in British Columbia. Because of the Australian market two more newsprint mills are being established, doubling the production of the Pacific province.
Lack of markets has hampered development otf the immense resources of British Columbia. It is credited with having available more than 285,000,000 coTds of pulpwood, consisting chiefly of spruce, western hemlock and balsam. As recently as 1910 not a ton of pulp or paper was manufactured in the province. To-day it ranks next to Ontario and Quebec, with a capital investment of some $41,000,000, giving employment to more than 2,500 persons. The two existing mills are turning out 200 tons of newsprint per day, and this

The Budget-Mr. Stork
will be doubled when the two new mills are operating. It is estimated that the value of this product iwill shortly reach $20,000,000 a year, much of it finding its way to Australia.
This is further evidence of the beneficial effect of the Australian treaty on British Columbia. In the county of Skeena, which I have the honour to represent, there is one of the finest pulp and paper plants to be found anywhere on .the North American continent. It is located at Ocean Falls, and I am credibly informed that the proprietors intend still further to extend their buildings.
The Australian treaty also gives a market for the fish canned in British Columbia. I assert that this government has done more to promote the fishing industry of my province than any preceding government. The budget places sheet tin, which is used in the manufacture of cans, on the free list, thus giving further benefit to one of our basic industries. The county of Skeena is an extensive area and contains vast natural wealth, fishing being one of its basic industries. In this connection I wish to place on Hansard some statistics which I have received to-day from the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and from which it will be apparent that my constituency produces a great deal of the fish taken in the province. I have said, Mr. Speaker, that this government has done a great deal for the development of the fishing industry of British Columbia. In 1922 a commission was appointed to investigate the whole of the fishing industry, both halibut and salmon, and every phase of the question was investigated. It was felt that the industry was so important, that so many interests were involved and so many men required consideration, that in place of bringing them all to Ottawa a commission should tour the province and in that way consider every angle of the situation. That commission was very successful; sittings were held in every part of British Columbia, 191 witnesses were examined and a report brought in which was adopted by the government of the day. As a result, the tax on canneries was reduced from $500 to $20; the tax on purse seines was reduced from $300 to $20; the tax on drag seines was reduced from $50 to $20, and the tax of one-half cent per fish caught in seines was abolished. This one item alone meant a tremendous increase in revenue to those engaged in the fishing industry. The license fee was reduced from $5 to $1; the duty on gas engines used for fishing boats was reduced; nets, twine and gear were placed on the free list; the use of gas boats was authorized-

speechtext:
I think I am correct. At
any rate, the use of gas boats was authorized for the first time on the Naas and Skeena rivers. Prior to to that the old method had been employed, while gas boats had been permitted on the Fraser river and in other parts ' of British Columbia. In the north they were still compelled to do their work by those methods which had obtained on the sea of Galilee some two thousand years ago. The fishermen of that country are now permitted to pursue their calling in safety by use of the modern gas boat. A policy was also adopted by the government placing the fishing industry solely in the hands of whites
The Budget-Mr. Stork

and native Indians. In 1923 there was a reduction of 40 per cent in fishing licenses granted to others than whites and native Indians; in the year following there was a further reduction of 15 per cent along that line, and now the total elimination of others than whites and native Indians is definitely in sight.
In the matter of old age pensions I know of no class of citizens which will hail the advent of such a bill with greater delight than will those fishermen who go down to the sea in ships and elce out a hard livelihood. They grow old quickly in the fishing game, esepecially on the stormy, rock-bound coast of the north Pacific, and those men will welcome the announcement that an old age pension system is to be brought into force.
In 1911, Mr. Speaker, we had an election in this country, held in connection with a reciprocity arrangement. The real issues of that election were lost sight of, and the slogan of our friends opposite became, "No truck or trade with the Yankees." Our American friends to the south naturally heard the people of Canada repeating that slogan, and said, "That is fair enough; we will have no truck or trade with the Canadians," and as a result we now have the Fordney tariff. We have heard a good deal recently about this "brick for brick" policy, but it seems to me to be a question of a brickbat for a brickbat, and the first brickbat thrown hit the fishermen on the Skeena river right in the eye. The high tariff has no supporters in the county of Skeena. I have just placed on Hansard a table showing the tremendous amount of halibut taken from the north Pacific, and the people who are catching halibut are free traders; the high tariff _ makes no hit with them. They are shipping this vast amount of halibut largely to the American market; it goes out over the Canadian National railways in refrigerators cars and contributes largely to the revenues of the Canadian National, since each refrigerator car earns about $1,000 in the transportation of fish.
But we are under a very grievous disadvantage ^ in connection with this market. Halibut is sold in the open market by auc- * fdon, and our Canadian fishermen receive two cents per pound less than do the American fishermen who market their catch in that port. All the fish are supposed to be destined for the American market; the buyer, anticipating that he will have to pay the two cent duty, deducts that amount from the price paid the fisherman. Thus this duty of two cents per pound has been for some time

a burning question with those people. Negotiations have been carried on and are still in progress, and we urgently and earnestly hope that they will result in the abolition of this duty.
As a result of the improvement in the fishing industry we find two new canneries being built in the northern part of the county of Skeena, and there is also a newly established biological station, put into operation by the Department of Marine and Fisheries for the study of fish life and the general advantage of the trade. At that station they are discovering new varieties and new species of fish. I have lived for a long time in the north country. I have been in the province of British Columbia for some thirty-seven years, and there are varieties of fish there of which I have never heard before. Only last fall, over on the north shore of Queen Charlotte islands, I found a brand new industry. At a little town called Tow Hill there has been established a new clam canning factory. When we speak of clams we all have in our mind's eye the old style of shell which litters the ocean beach, but this particular clam which they are developing at Tow Hill is a brand new variety, and I would imagine it to be the aristocrat of the clam tribe. It is enclosed in a case which looks very much like a spectacle case that a man might use, made of tortoise shell. The shells are as thin as paper, beautiful in finish and colour, about 7 inches long and If inches wide, with the ends rounded. They make a very beautiful looking shell. These clams are of such a quality that there is an unlimited market for them. It is something entirely new. This is just one instance of what can be procured by scientific research, by investment and by the far-sightedness of the people who live in that country.
I discovered while I was at Tow Hill that they have there one of the finest natural beaches, I should think, on the known globe to-day. It has been my good fortune to have visited the beaches in California, the sands at Blackpool and Ostend, and I say without hesitation that on the north shore of Queen Charlotte islands is a sand beach as hard as a cement floor, fifty miles in extent-the greatest natural speedway that one could find anywhere. Fifty, yes, one hundred, automobiles could race along this speedway for fifty miles, and I am sure that when Sir Henry Thornton gets his eye on this locality, with his desire to attract world tourists and build up the Canadian National railway, when he brings to bear his activity on that section of the country, we shall have an improved steamboat service from Prince

The Budget-Mr. Stork
Rupert to Alaska via the Queen Charlotte islands. This beach I speak of is one of the greatest natural advantages, I think, which the whole of the north country possesses. If Burns or Byron had visited such a spot, it would be interesting to see what they would have produced in the way of description of what I regard as one of the greatest wonders of the North American continent.
Seventeen years ago, in the town of Prince Rupert, Sir Charles Rivers Wilson, who was then the president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company and also of its subsidiary the Grand Trunk Pacific, made a speech in which he said he regretted the fact that he was an old man with not many more years to live, but that even at his age he hoped to see before he died the fulfilment of the project of the Grand Trunk Pacific. He said he hoped to see going out of the port of Prince Rupert the trade and traffic of the western prairies, and coming back through that port the wealth of the Orient. This grand old man has long since passed to his rest. The defeat of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1911, the death of Charles M. Hays, the change of government in 1911, the stress of war, the further fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific had its throat cut by Mackenzie and Mann,-due to all these things the development of that great country has been temporarily arrested. There was a period of stagnation between 1911 and 1921, but, Sir, under the present Prime Minister, and under the genius of Sir Henry Thornton, this country is now beginning to be developed, and with the tremendous improvement in the situation of the Canadian National Railways, as stated in the budget, and with the improvement of the Grand Trunk Pacific, we can look forward to the future as being bright and promising.
Before I resume my seat I wish to deal for one moment with a matter which received a great deal of adverse criticism and unfavourable advertisement during the last election campaign. From every Tory newspaper in the Dominion of Canada and from every Tory platform throughout this country there was hurled at the Prince Rupert elevator the charge that it was one of the crimes of the Mackenzie King government. Even in the recent by-election in Middlesex, if I am correctly informed, the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) took further occasion to refer to this matter. Our Conservative friends, who have had so much to say in denunciation of this proposition, ought to remember that within three months of the day they came into office in 1911 their first act in this despised town of Prince Rupert was
to expropriate from their own friends 100 feet of frontage on Third avenue, at a price, set by their own board of arbitrators, of $95,000. Then out of the native rock they chiselled a basement at an additional cost of $25,000. We have a very wet climate in that part of the country, and this post office site was so located that it acted as a drain pool for the surrounding land, with the result that this basement filled up with water. Then our loyal friends who think so much of Prince Rupert installed an electric pump, operated by one of their own friends. This pump would work night and day pumping out the water, and those of us in the north country who were doing what we could to keep up our courage during the dark days of the war had our courage renewed and our spirits revived by listening night and day to the patriotic heart throbs of the Tory pump working in the government cellar. When they criticize this Prince Rupert elevator they ought to say that they themselves in 1911 gave the people of that north country reason to hope that they had located in a place that would be advantageous. Let me say that this elevator at Prince Rupert has been completed now only a matter of seven or eight weeks. The sawdust and the shavings have scarcely been removed, but still things are moving. The elevator there will be used. The dream of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the speech of Sir Charles Rivers Wilson, and the hope of Charles M. Hays will yet be realized. The elevator at Prince Rupert will hold grain that will be exported shortly to the Orient, and in return there will come back to the Canadian National railways for transportation to the east the silk of Japan and of China, and other oriental wealth. The prophecy of the grand old man who has gone to his rest is coming true. It is coming true rapidly, and it is heartening to pioneers of that northern country who have staked their all, and who are living in the hope of seeing the completion of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and of witnessing the prosperity that is bound to come in time to the whole of the northern part of the province of British Columbia.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that any tariff introduced into this House should be based on the principle of protection. In my opinion a proper application of the principle of protection will solve all the economic ills of every province in the Dominion from Vancouver to Halifax. I believe in protection as a principle, not as a privilege. I do not believe in
The Budget-Mr. Church

can prove anything by figures. Then fourth, is the stabilization of currency. They have not accomplished anything in that line. The fifth item is the reorganization of industry. They have accomplished nothing in this regard. There is no way of reversing the order of these steps or of skipping a step. Progress in each stage depends absolutely upon a complete fulfilment of the requirements of the stage preceding. By the application of this yardstick one may be aided in distinguishing between those disturbances Which strike at the foundations of the economic structure and those which represent merely some house cleaning in the upper stories. As I say they failed on all points.
Then I say that a safeguarding of industries act should be applied as a principle to our raw material instead of our exporting them to the United States, to have them manufactured there into the finished product and shipped back to this country for sale. As I said before, unemployment in this country is due to the fact that we have failed to develop our own natural resources and to conserve our own raw material. We are exporting in the raw and crude state to the United States various materials that we could manufacture at home. Take for example the case of asbestos; we are sending out $6,000,000 worth of raw asbestos taken from the bowels of the earth in Quebec, and that material when manufactured in the United States yields a return of some $75,000,000. We are exporting mica, nickel, pulpwood, power and coal. If we manufactured or utilized these articles in this country, it would provide work for tens of thousands of men. Canada supplied 85 per cent of the mica of the world, and 95 per cent to the United States. In 1924 Canada sold 112,000 tons of mica to the United States in the mill fibre state, only one degree removed from the crude. For that we received $5,546,000. When that was manufactured in the United States, it realized $70,000,000 worth of the finer products of asbestos, and another $10,000,000 worth of rough asbestos. Had we developed our own mica, $80,000,000 would have been distributed among Canadians.
Canada controls the world's supply of nickel. We need fear no competition in this particular article. We should develop nickel in our own country and help provide employment here. Canada's great nickel deposits give the United States all its supply and the world 85 per cent of its supply. Canada is limping along on a low tariff while the United States grows prosperous on a high tariff, three times as high as ours. The United States controls seventy-

five per cent of the silk business of the world and seventy-five per cent of the rubber manufacturing, and yet not an ounce of rubber oi silk raw materials is produced in that country. A proper protective tariff would induce growth and expansion here as nothing else in the world could.
No one knows better than the grain growers in the west what need there is for some change in our system. Their grain is being taken across the line to Buffalo where there are now twenty-eight elevators, and it is being milled there, mixed with American wheat and exported overseas, while the identity of Canada's fine hard wheat is destroyed. All the employment that is furnished by those twenty-eight elevators in Buffalo would give work to
15.000	men at Port 'Colborne and other lake Ontario points, if a duty and embargo were placed up to 45 per cent on wheat, having it milled in Canada and exported entirely through Canadian channels. I am glad that we are getting some converts in this regard, one hon. member to my left having advocated this policy.
We are certainly not developing our natural resources in this country as we should, for if we manufactured our mica and utilized our power and our coal in this country we could provide work for tens of thousands of men. Last year Canada sold 4,350,000 cords of pulp-wood to the United States, receiving $13,000,000 for it, while this raw pulpwood was converted in the United States into a value of $67,000,000. We sent one-third as cordwood, one-third as pulp, and one-third as paper. We are also sending $100,000,000 every year to the mine owners in Pennsylvania. We could use $56,000,000 of that sum to provide work and wages in the Maritime provinces, in Alberta and in central Canada. And do not forget that Canada on the other side of the account buys back the manufactured products of these raw mineral materials which are manufactured in other countries. Do not forget that copper, as a raw material, is being exported in bulk and is being manufactured in the United States into articles worth millions of dollars. For example, I know a large firm in Toronto which last Christmas purchased
30.000	radio machines made in New York, Boston and Providence, and the best parts of these sets were manufactured from Canadian copper. Last year Great Britain purchased about 145,000 tons of copper, and Germany took three times that amount.
The Liberal government have done everything by fits and starts; they have not ac-

The Budget-Mr. Church
complished anything with the tariff. The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) did not approach the subject from the standpoint of the Liberal platform of 1893, because not one of the planks of that platform has been carried out. Hon. Alexander Mackenzie said:
There is no .policy more consistent with what we call the dark ages of the world than that of protection as a principle.
I would apply protection as a principle all over the country. He says further:
There is no principle more consistent with the advance of human freedom, no principle more in accordance with the great prosperity which prevails in our time, than that of absolute freedom of commerce.
Here is a quotation from a speech of Sir Wilfrid Laurier at the Liberal convention in Winnipeg. He said:
If the National Policy had any basis at all it was that the bread of the peopile should be taxed. It was an inhuman policy that would make bread and fuel dearer. It as always easy to increase the tariff because by so doing you increase the private fortunes of certain individuals.
We stand for freedom. I denounce the policy of protection as bondage-yes bondage; and I refer to bondage in the same manner in which American slavery was bondage; not in the same degree, perhaps, but in the same manner. In the same manner the people of Canada, the inhabitants of the city of Winnipeg especially, are toiling for a master who takes away not every cent of profit but a very large percentage, a very large portion of your earnings for which you sweat and toil.
I will not quote any further regarding that particular convention, but on the tariff issue the Liberals of this country have never had a settled policy since Sir Wilfrid Laurier was their leader in 1897. The principles of Liberalism of which we hear so much from! the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Mackenzie King) produced this state of affairs. It has been a disturbance in the economic life of the nation. The principles of Liberalism, so often on the lips of Mackenzie King, were faithfully applied by him to the tariff question and produced a bluff designed solely to fool a sufficient number of the electors to get into office. There was never any real concern in the mind of Mr. King, as there was never any in the mind of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, of a stable tariff for Canada. The Progressive movement in western Canada has been betrayed by its leaders, who are Liberals first. The sincere Progressives backed the movement in protest against Sir Wilfrid Laurier's failure to carry out his promises of free trade. But the leaders who came to the front in the Progressive party were men with feet of clay. They fell quite readily into the traps set by the Liberals. Instead of punishing the Liberal party, which
furnished the sole reason for starting the Progressive movement, the Progressives have proved themselves a prop and a stay to give the Liberal party a longer lease on life. The only difference between the two is the difference between tweedledum and tweedledee.
I believe the National Policy should further be applied to the patent law of this country. If j'ou look over the Dominion patent office records you will find that a vast number of patents are held by Americans; they come over here Monday, leave on Tuesday with a patent, and go home to the United States and manufacture under the patent. That applies to patents for engines and motor cars. I w:sh to draw the attention of the House to a great grievance in this connection, to an evil that is wrought in any country against its labour and which is every day working in Canada. Our patent laws are absurd. They are pro-American and anti-Canadian; that is all they are. They are very injurious to the labour interests of Canada and have the effect of sending our workmen to the United States. The patent law is framed in a way to give the benefit to all those outside of Canada rvhile our labourers in Canada are suffering. In the majority of the patents granted in the Dominion patent protection is given to persons outside of this country, and the products to which they relate are made or manufactured and shipped in to Canada, giving no labour in the making or manufacturing of the same to the workers of this country-just a case of dump, dump, dump under the protection of the so-called patent law. That is a nice kind of patent law for a national policy country like Canada. Books, periodicals, magazines and a host of other printed matter printed in other countries and having copyright protection in this country are shipped here involving no more labour in Canada than transportation and distribution. A number of automobile manufacturers with patents are only assembling the cars here, giving the labour of making the parts to workmen in other countries.
Machinery of all descriptions, household articles, wearing apparel and other articles toe numerous to mention are patented here and made elsewhere. In regard to chemical processes for the refining of minerals, the raw material is shipped from Canada to the United States to be refined and the finished product is shipped back to this country. Why can that refining not be done in Canada? There is direct and indirect labour involved in the manufacture of all these articles and other countries are reaping the full benefit of
The Budget-Mr. Church

having the labour done by their workmen. I understand that ninety per cent of the patents, trade marks and copyrights that are granted in Canada are granted to persons outside of Canada who manufacture these articles and ship them to this country. This is not a square deal to either our labour or our industries, and as long as this state of thing continues we shall have a large number of our workmen out of employment involving in labour and business a loss of thousands of millions of dollars annually to the Dominion.

The Toronto Star would cease publication, either because support was withdrawn by the merchants whose custom was being driven from Toronto, or because there would not be enough policemen in Detroit to protect the Star's place of publication against the women who sought a reckoning with the sheet that had served as champion of a policy that took the jobs away from their husbands and drove them into a foreign land.

Since the beginning of the present debate, Mr. Speaker, I have listened to many speeches, and I find that we are now in the very same situation as that in which we have found ourselves for several days. The speech just delivered by the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) does not differ from other speeches we have heard, except to the extent that he was possibly more prolific, and if I should attempt to follow him in all the details of his address it would probably take me as long as it took him, namely about two hours and a half. The hon. member dealt with many subjects, going from doctors to coal mines, from coal mines to lawyers and other professional men, and so on, in such a way that it would be impossible for me to answer him in a short time. I hope, however, in the course of my remarks to express in a general way my own views in the matter and generally to answer what he said during the course of his speech.
My remarks will be very brief, and they would be much shorter were it not for the fact that I have a few quotations to make in respect to the general situation, and especially with reference to railway conditions affecting the city of Quebec, coupled with Maritime rights; for to my mind these two are one and the same.
I am not in the habit of paying useless compliments to anyone, and I do not intend
to do so on the present occasion. However, we have to face the proposals as presented by the government in the budget and either accept or reject them.

to point, to an unusually large expansion of foreign commerce during the recently ended fiscal year. There was a surplus of revenue over expenditure of nearly $34,000,000 in the year's operations, a reduction of net debt of $22,353,000, and a marked increase in the operating profits of the Canadian National Railways, these having amounted to $30,443,000 in the calendar year of 1925 or about $13,000,000 more than in the preceding year.
The foreign trade of Canada continues to mount both in volume and value. In the year ended March 31, this commerce reached the very considerable sum of $2,258,500,000, of which $1,330,000,000 was made up of exports and $927,000,000 of imports, the favourable balance thus being $402,695,000. So large a credit in the external trade of the year has been a potential factor in restoring Canadian currency to par.
Domestic business has not presented any novel factors durihg the current month, but the condition remains more satisfactory than in recent years and the spirit of confidence in the future appears to grow. Commodity prices are fairly steady and would appear to have been pegged about 60 per cent over a pre-war average, with inevitable fluctuation in price of one or other commodity. Railway car loadings and railway earnings are in excess of last year. Business mortality in the first quarter of 1926 was substantially less than in the corresponding quarter of the previous year, the number of failures declining from 669 to 593, with aggregate liabilities down from $10,683,000 to $7,566,000.
The estimated quantity of Canadian wheat remaining in Canada at April 1st was 161,376,000 bushels or 40,000,000 bushels greater than on the corresponding date in 1925, which fact gives promise of an active shipping season, and continued expansion of export trade. Building operations the Dominion over are much in excess of last year. It is too early in the season to forecast agricultural production but the acreage to be sown in the three western provinces this year will be practically the same as last. Live stock has wintered well and expectation as that the steady growth in the cattle export trade since the removal of the British embargo will not be interrupted. Cold weather has somewhat delayed farming operations in the eastern provinces. Immigration gives indication of reaching a larger volume than for a considerable time past. Taken as a whole, it *can be said that the bright spots in the business situation greatly predominate.
The article is fair to all, and covers every one of the provinces. Speaking of Quebec, it uses these words:
Quebec-Winter logging operations, which have been generally on a reduced scale, are finished and logs are ready for the drive. The lumber market remains quiet, Pacific coast stocks dominating the situation. The price and demand for pulpwood continues to hold up well and it is anticipated that the increased production in newsprint this year will easily be absorbed. There has not been any appreciable change in the price of staple commodities, apart from butter and eggs, which show seasonal declines, and potato prices, which are unusually strong. Trade, both wholesale and retail, has been adversely affected by the lateness of spring. The manufacturing situation indicates improvement. Orders generally are in excess of last year and a number of plants formerly only partially operating are now running on full time. Collections are moderately satisfactory.
What about Ontario?
Ontario.-Wholesale houses are enjoying a slightly improved volume of trade compared with last year.

Retail sales of seasonable Easter goods, however, were retarded by inclement weather. Collections are being satisfactorily met. Work on the land will commence a fortnight later than a year ago. There is an abundance of moisture, fall wheat has wintered well, and conditions from the agricultural viewpoint are propitious. Farmers' dispersal sales are marked by good attendance and good prices, and milch cows are in special demand. Industry as a whole is more active. Pulp and paper companies continue to produce at capacity. Agricultural implement manufacturers are busy, and finished steel companies are well employed. Recent reductions in the tariff on motor cars make it necessary for manufacturers to submit the changes embodied in the budget to an intensive study before they are able to gauge the full effects. With the advent of open weather, activity in the northern mining camps is increasing.
This article gives a fairly comprehensive view of the situation. It contains similar paragraphs in regard to the prairie provinces, the Maritime provinces and British Columbia, showing that conditions to-day under the present government are very good.

That paper was published in Montreal. I tried to find one published in another province, in a city-Toronto-which is probably the business rival of Montreal. This is what the Monetary Times has to say under date April 23, one day after the publication of the article which 1 have just quoted:
1926 Budget Is Popular. Is It Wise?
That the tax changes proposed by the Dominion government are popular is quite evident. Whether they are sound depends upon future developments.
The country demanded a reduction in taxes, and it has got at. Every one has felt the pinch of Dominion government taxation, and the immediate effect of the changes is a saving to nearly every one. The government could scarcely have taken a more popular course. The income tax is o-f direct interest to a large proportion of the thinking citizens of Canada, and the reductions mean a great saving to the middle classes on the support of which any party in this country depends. The repeal of the stamp tax on receipts, the return to penny postage and the reductions in the sales tax are also of widespread interest.
While there promises to be some debate about the income tax, the one important snag in the programme seems to be the reductions in automobile duties. The other tariff changes are by no means negligible, but apparently only one vital spot in industry has been touched. We are being told that the industry cannot subsist with only 20 per cent protection It is difficult ito believe that in an industry of such proportions, where even in Canada benefits of large scale operations can be realized, it is not possible to do business here (with this margin. But some of the statements issued by manufacturers are quite definite, and while sales should be enlarged through the reductions in prices there is no doubt but that the volume of production in Canada will be lower. It is evident that automobile duties are a crucial point in the

The Budget-Mr. Parent
government's podicy, and it will have to see its proposals through or forever hold its peace on tariff reduction.
The serious aspect is that of national revenue. Tax reduction at the present time does not augur well for tax reduction in the future. It is only through a steady surplus of revenue over expenditure that we can reduce debt, strengthen our national balance sheet and reduce taxes with safety later on. With revenue keeping up, expenditure cut down, and the National railways doing better, the government had just got into a comfortable position. But the contest between the parties is so keen at the present time that the government has evidently felt the necessity of immediately capitalizing its savings. The 1926 budget is one which will probably ,be of great political import, it certainly is going to be a weighty factor in our national finances.
I cannot be accused of having quoted any papers with partisan views. I have quoted two of the most serious publications that have dealt with the situation.
Coming to the details mentioned in these articles, I have no doubt that the people of Canada will be satisfied with the news that a reduction of taxation to the extent of $25,000,000 will be spread over the country generally. The reduction in the postal rate, bringing us back to the days of Sir William Mulock, brings pleasant memories to the Liberals who were in the House at that time. The reduction then made was so well accepted that I have no doubt the present reduction will be popular and well received throughout the Dominion. The stamp tax on receipts was an annoying tax for everyone, from the humblest to the highest, and its abolition will no doubt be appreciated by the community at large.
The changes in the income tax law should perhaps be the subject of some more lengthy remarks. I fully realize that the men who have been working on this particular question have given it a good deal of attention and study. At the same time, even the best men that Canada can produce may not have at first seen all the trouble that such a tax involves, and I intend to put before the government for further study these few considerations. Let us take the case of a close corporation where a man has been spending ten or fifteen years of his life in establishing an industry. He may have been working under a company name, although the owner of the whole business. What is the result under the tax as proposed in the budget? That man will be taxed first nine per cent on the income of the company; that is a reduction of one per cent from what it was previously. On his own income or dividend from the operation of the company he will be taxed a second time. Perhaps he and two or three of his companions who have invested
money in that company will be in receipt of dividends therefrom; and in that case they will be taxed a further sum on that amount. I do not think the government had in view the taxing of a person twice under those conditions, as the present budget proposes. That is a point to which I wanted to draw the attention of the government, because it touches more people than one might think at first sight. I can understand that the law might apply with good results to many companies listed on the stock exchange where a man can buy and sell without caring whether he gets a dividend or not, but I hardly think it is fair for a man who has invested his money in a company which ho built up himself should be taxed twice when others are taxed only once.

speechtext:
The hon. member can wait until I vote and then he will find out. Take the case of a mining company: every time jou take anything out of the mine the capital is reduced. Under the law as it stands an allowance is made for depreciation by reason of the fact that in operating the mine you draw upon your capital. If you happen to be part owner of the mine the company first pays the income tax, and as shareholder or part owner you must also pay, so that whereas you are given consideration for depreciation onfy once you must pay the tax twice. I am putting these facts before the House simply to point out to the government that it is always rather dangerous to make changes in tariff matters. If we can maintain a certain stability I think it will be better for all concerned. I have no doubt that the government is keeping this in mind and that in the creation of the tariff board it means to protect industry in Canada to a reasonable extent, without enabling fictitious industries to exist at the expense of the consuming public.
The budget refers to the fact that the Canadian National Railways are this year submitting a satisfactory report which discloses some $30,000,000 to the good after operating expenses have been taken into account. I do not intend to discuss the railway situation in detail but I want to refer to the pledges given by previous governments to the city from which I come in regard to the Transcontinental railway and its terminal. May I in passing offer my hearty congratulations to the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) upon the motion which he

The Budget-Mr. Parent
submitted to the House the other day? That motion was in the interests of the Dominion as a whole and particularly of the ports of Quebec, Halifax and St. John. In my opinion the surplus money in the hands of the Canadian National Railways could, if properly spent, provide Quebec with a suitable terminal. I dislike very much going back to the election of 1904 and discussing the campaign that was fought then. The whole issue was the construction of the Transcontinental railway. Two companies were trying to secure the right to build a line from the Atlantic to the Pacific, one company being known as the Transcona and the other the Transcontinental. The Transcontinental was the one whose terms Sir Wilfrid Laurier accepted, and the whole question was thoroughly discussed in the session of 1903, when all the facts were clearly laid before the Canadian people. It was stated over and over again in 1903 that the main purpose of constructing that line was to transport the grain of the western provinces through Canadian territory to the Canadian ports of Quebec, Halifax and St. John. No considerable opposition was offered at the time, but of course in a matter of this kind, as in any similar matter, the moment some people saw that there was a possibility of their own interests being affected, politics was introduced, with the result that criticism was indulged in throughout the country. This criticism went on for a few years while the construction work was in progress, until the election of 1908, when the issue was again the wisdom or unwisdom of constructing the Transcontinental railway. In that election the people of Canada declared it to be their will that this railwas' should be built for the purpose, as had always been understood, of transporting the grain of the west through Canadian territory to the ports I have mentioned. Then came the election of 1911 when unfortunately there was a change of government. There were those who could not see eye to eye with Sir Wilfrid Laurier and who condemned the undertaking. They uesd every possible means at their disposal to prevent the construction of that line, and if there is one city in Canada which more than any other resented the stand which was then taken by the opponents of this railway it was the city which I have the honour to represent, the city of Quebec. Anyone who looks down from the Chateau Frontenac to-day upon the present station, which was put up in place of one that should have cost in the neighbourhood of 1800,000, cannot help feeling that this unsightly structure is nothing if not an insult to a government which had the courage to

carry through so stupendous an undertaking as the Transcontinental railway. Quebec was induced, on the strength of promises solemnly given that city, to tear down a building valued at some $250,000 and to hand over to the Dominion of Canada a site worth $2,000,000 for the purpose of erecting thereon a station which was to cost, as I have said, about $800,000. What did the city get as a matter of fact? A building that is not worth $20,000 and which moreover is so ugly that in my opinion the Canadian National Railways would be doing the people of Quebec, and for that matter of the Dominion, a real service by tearing it down.
