Here now follows a summary of the engagements undertaken by the government:
1.	The commission undertakes to spend a sum of at least two millions of dollars (apart from the cost of the land to'be purchased or expropriated for the railway) to build on the said land or in the vicinity thereof a station, sheds, warehouses, workshops, et cetera. Said workshops to be the most considerable of the Transcontinental railway in the province of Quebec;
Everyone understands, Mr. Speaker, that certain of these works had to be delayed on account of the war period, and the people of the city of Quebec realized quite well that during that period immense works of im-

The Budget-Mr. Parent
portance could not be proceeded with. But now, if the railways can find money elsewhere to do work similar to this, I think it would be . in their interests to carry out those pledges already given.
It has been stated that the .province of Quebec as a whole was very much against the nationalization of railways. Part of this statement is true and part of it has no foundation of truth whatever. As a matter of fact it has always been an open question in the province of Quebec as elsewhere, but certain persons who were against the nationalization of railways seem to have arrived at other conclusions, and I am glad to 'be able to read an article from L'Action Sociale Catholique of May 3 of this year:
(Translation): Aoconding to the Hast Dominion budget as well as to the monthflv reports of the Canadian Nationail Railway Board, our State railways are in a better financial situation. We are fled to hope that before flonig the while elephant will no more be a drag on the country's Treasury.
No one will, for a moment, douibt that the greatest share in this success belongs to Sir Henry Thornton. He .placed at the disposal of our National Raiilways bis great ability, a training very seldom encountered, a great knowledge of railway matters, an unquestionable good will.
And ill is efforts have been crowned by success. Those who selected him had a very happy thought. There is no doubt about it.

If Sir Henry Thornton has really endeavoured to obtain the co-operation of the Canadian people, as he would be expected to do so as to attain success, we must say that this co-operation was not denied to him.
The French Canadian people were opposed to State ownership of railways known, to-day, by the name of Canadian National Raff ways, as they woiild be opposed to-morrow to any scheme of State ownership which would include the Canadian Pacific Railway. They have no faith in the efficiency of such a system, they are rather convinced of its dangers. Experience, pointing out, to the little success, generally of State ownership undertakings, sides with them.
They were therefore opposed to State ownership. This State ownership for reasons of irretrievable errors or otherwise was decided upon anyway. It has been for the last few years an accomplished fact.
We possess certain quadifications not understood by a great number of Canadians of different origin. Among them there is one which urges us on to begin a contest long before the others because we never lose sight of the principles upon which everything rests. Others who think themesdlves more practical, do not bother much about these principfles; facts control their actions. And as facts always proceed from applied principles, often, if they make a move, it is only long after us.

In any case, State ownership having been agreed upon, there either remained for us to make the best of it *or let the country go into bankruptcy. We unhesitatingly put our shoulder to -the wheel, and this [DOT]the mor6 willingly because of the great ability of the man appointed as head of the National Railways.
The French Canadians gave to the Board of National -Railways their full support, they put their trust in
its President. Their efforts were of some account in the improvement obtained; no douibt Should exist in that connection in the minds of the members of the National Railway Board.
We therefore have reason to expect that our cooperation will be appreciated in a still more practical way, and that if they are willing to accept our "lending a hand" at the bottom of the ladder, we shall expect also, when the opportunity presents itself to cooperate in the higher spheres.
The Canadian National railways, in 1924, had a staff of 101 officers. Out of that number, there are but two Frertdh Canadians. Moreover, if the latter hold posi tions of some importance, we have yet no one to represent us on the Board of Directors. Our numerical importance, the unhesitating co-operation we Send in the improvement of our National railways, is deserving of better treatment.

It is not a question of removals or of asking for dismissals of officials. The higher officials of the National Railways are jflaced there, no doubt, owing to their personal merits and the eminent services they render. Moreover, we do not stoop to such means.
We simply ask that when the next vacancy occurs- we have no idea when-in the Board of the C.N.R., it be filled by a representative of the French Canadian element. As no indications exist that such a thing may happen to-day or to-morrow, we have no name to suggest. If it is the intention to act fairly towards us to-morrow, it is easy to start paving the way immediately.
This is the request we address to Sir Henry Thornton. Perhaps, the thing has already been done, we have no knowledge of it. If not, it is more than time to think of it.
We would feel wounded if we were to be kept out forever from the higher spheres of the C.N.R. Board of directors.
We have a right to be there and we are able to fill the position.
With the exception of a few corrections this article represents my views very well, but the article is not well informed when it states that the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways has no French Canadian representative. For the information of this newspaper I may say that I believe both Mr. Decary and Colonel Talbot, of the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways, are French Canadians. But the remarks of this article might be amplified, and I think in fairness to my compatriots I may fairly say without fear of contradiction that, since the French Canadians represent about one quarter of the total population of Canada, the number of representatives in various offices and positions on the Canadian National Railways does not represent a fair proportion. I suggest to the government that in considering future appointments, qualified French Canadians-and we have many such- be considered. I might go further, Mr. Speaker, and apply the same remarks to the civil service. I was looking over the telephone book of the House of Commons the other day, comprising all the departments; I take it for granted that those who have

telephones for their own use are those who have acquired the highest positions. Take the whole telephone book; look it over from beginning to end and see how many French names are contained therein; then compare that proportion with the population of Canada. I do not say this to raise any question of prejudice: that never entered my mind, and I hope never will.
With these remarks, Mr. Speaker, I repeat that on the whole I am quite satisfied with the proposals as presented by the government to-day, and I shall have no hesitation at all in supporting the budget. It is indeed a fact that certain industries may suffer for the present. The automobile industry may suffer temporarily, but if we consider the situation in a broad-minded way; if we realize that these industries have been over-capitalized -though it is possible that the younger men who are in charge of the industry to-day may find it harder to make that capital valuable than those who started the industry-when we take into consideration the fact that Canada is rapidly increasing in prosperity and that we are receiving immigrants in largely increasing numbers, we believe, and we think we are right in our contention, that in a short time these younger men in charge to-day, with their courage and their optimism, will find that their industries are doing better perhaps than they have ever done before. In a word, to sum up, circumstances are such that the budget means co-operation of the west with the east, Ontario being the connecting link to sell its manufactured products from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad indeed of this opportunity to say a word of very hearty congratulation to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (M!r. Robb) for the excellent manner in which he presented his budget speech of some three weeks ago. Delivered with all the urbanity which is so characteristic of the hon. minister, his speech was marked by brevity and clarity to an extent that made it indeed a treat to hear. To listen to such a clear and concise presentation was indeed a treat to me, and one which I shall long remember. Those of us who have not been in this House before, but who have followed, from without, public doings and parliamentary procedure, will remember well the budget speeches of former days which occupied, not less than an hour, as did the present one, but often two, three, four or even five hours. The present distinguished Minister of Finance has set an example to the members of this House, an example which in the interest of

time and the despatch of public business should be scrupulously followed. I have always felt that apart from the leaders of the parties, the ministers, and those directly interested in some particular matter of importance, the speeches of individual members should be curtailed, for the result would be a contraction of the altogether too prolonged sessions of this House of Commons.
